ORCHID: https://orcid.org/0000-0003-4529-0593

My research examines party group switching, political representation and party institutionalization in the European Parliament. Below are my two published journal articles as well as the data and replication code.

Originally, I did all of my analysis using Stata. The downloads include those original Stata materials.
Because I myself no longer have an institutional affiliation or a Stata license, I used AI to convert the Stata .dta files into CSVs and port the analysis code to Python. The original Stata logs are retained as references for checking the results.
These converted files can be opened in Python, R or other statistical software.
I did initial replication checks using the converted CSVs and Python scripts to make sure that the conversion was accurate, and the results are also posted.
Each Python package includes its input data, code, saved outputs and documentation, so a Stata licence is not needed to use it.

## This too in moderation

**Evaluating the effect of delegate dissatisfaction on ambitious party group switching in the European Parliament**

Aaron R. Martin. *Party Politics* **29**(4), 726–740 (2023; first published online in 2022).

This article examines whether the most dissatisfied members are also the most likely to change party groups. The analysis finds that moderate ideological outliers have the highest odds of an ambitious switch, while the most extreme outliers are less likely to leave.

[Read the article](https://doi.org/10.1177/13540688221096531){.btn .btn-primary .btn-sm}
[Article PDF](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1177/13540688221096531){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm}

## Party group collapse and strategic switching

**Party group collapse and strategic switching in the European Parliament**

Aaron R. Martin. *European Union Politics* **22**(3), 521–544 (2021).

This article distinguishes strategic party group switches from changes forced by group collapse. It examines how group institutionalization and the policy distance between members, national delegations and party groups relate to switching during 1979–2009.

[Read the article](https://doi.org/10.1177/1465116521999718){.btn .btn-primary .btn-sm}
[Open access PDF](https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/77080/1/1465116521999718.pdf){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm}

**Replication scope:** the Python port includes data construction and selected statistical results. Its saved reports document comparisons with the original Stata datasets, Table 2 t-tests, Table 4 Firth models and Appendix B. Some figures, descriptive tables and robustness checks are outside the port's scope. See the included README for details and numerical tolerances.

## Using the data

Download an individual CSV to explore a dataset, or extract a complete Python package to run the archived analysis. For example:

```python
import pandas as pd

data = pd.read_csv("PP_dataset.csv", low_memory=False)
print(data.shape)
```

CSV files retain numeric category codes; the accompanying metadata provides label definitions. Dates are stored as text and empty fields represent missing values. CSV does not retain every Stata storage attribute or distinguish all of Stata's extended missing-value codes. Use the original `.dta` files when those details matter.

The CSV downloads were checked against their corresponding Stata files for dimensions, column names and cell values, with a small tolerance for numeric precision. Saved model-validation reports are supplied from the earlier replication work; packaging the downloads did not rerun the full statistical analyses.

Anyone can use the data for whatever they want, just please cite the appropriate articles (CC BY 4.0).
[Download checksums](downloads/checksums.json)

[Download the original report](downloads/party-politics/_multilevel_findings.md)

#### What the reported models actually are
Tables 4 and 5 are **three-level nested mixed-effects logits**, not two-level:

    xtmelogit <dv> <covariates> || start_group_num: || bloc_id3:

a random intercept for the EP party group (`start_group_num`, 25 groups) AND a
random intercept for the national-party delegation (`bloc_id3`) nested within it.
lme4 equivalent: `(1 | start_group_num/bloc_id3)`.

#### Ground truth (from march25_2021.log), Table 5 (amb_switch)

| Column | Model | logLik | key coefficients |
|--------|-------|--------|------------------|
| 4  | intensity | -563.988 | z_intense2 -0.3592, c_npd_perc -11.160, c_epg_perc -9.314, govt2 -0.7115, mep_tenure 0.3726, female -0.7780, _cons -5.6818 |
| 7  | quadratic | -513.389 | a1_std2 1.3359, a2_std2 0.6217, a1^2 -0.1782, a2^2 -0.0933, c_npd_perc -12.744 |
| 10 | full      | -493.246 | a1_std2 1.6026, a2_std2 0.8869, a1^2 -0.2034, a2^2 -0.1150 |

(The published `table5.txt` matches the intensity and quadratic columns exactly;
the "full" column differs slightly - 1.624 vs 1.6026 - suggesting the printed
table was assembled from a marginally different model run than this log.)

#### Reproduction status
- **Exact Stata outputs are preserved in the log**, so the results themselves are
  recoverable at full precision without Stata.
- **Independent reproduction was attempted in Python and did not succeed here:**
  a two-level fit is systematically ~20-40% attenuated (wrong structure), and the
  correct three-level nested fit could not be optimized within the sandbox's
  compute limit (nested quadrature is expensive; Stata itself hit "not concave"
  iterations, so the models are numerically delicate).
- **Recommended path:** run `make_pp_multilevel.R` (corrected to the nested
  `(1 | start_group_num/bloc_id3)` structure) in RStudio and compare its output to
  the ground-truth values above. `lme4` will be close but is not guaranteed to
  match Stata's `xtmelogit` to the decimal.

:::
